phases.title: The Family
phases.goal: Extend one good design into a family that holds together at every weight, width and size.
phases.why: A typeface is a family, not a set. The work of making a family is less about drawing new styles than about understanding which parts of the design were accidental.
phases.milestone: You have a bold, and it taught you something about your regular that you did not know.

lessons.title: The bold is a test of the system
lessons.objective: Draw a bold that exposes the weaknesses of your regular, and fix the regular first.

principles.title: The question is where the weight does not go
principles.body: Weight goes everywhere: to the left, to the right, and on top of some letters. Adding it only to the left and the right makes the bold wider than the light, which is jarring. A little extra x-height in the heavier weights compensates for that, and the change is almost invisible to the eye.

principles.title: Bolds need tighter spacing
principles.body: The counters of a bold are smaller, so the space between the letters has to shrink to keep the same relationship between inside and outside. A bold that is spaced like its regular looks heavy and clumsy.

principles.title: Drawing the bold first is a diagnostic
principles.body: Before you draw a regular, draw the bold. The bold will show you the terminals that are too weak, the joints that will not survive, and the counters that will close up. You can then fix the regular before you have spent a year on it.

principles.title: The optical extremes teach you the middle
principles.body: If your regular looks good but your black looks like a different typeface, the problem is usually one of the small decisions: a terminal that is too blunt, a joint that is too soft, a counter that is too small. The extremes show you which.

practice: Draw a black weight of your n and o before touching the rest of the alphabet. What breaks first?
Set your regular and your bold on the same line. Is the colour of the two blocks the same?
Take the tightest counter in your regular and thicken it. Does it survive?
checklist: My bold is not simply a wider version of my regular.
My bold is spaced tighter than my regular.
Drawing the bold taught me something and I changed the regular because of it.
Every counter in my bold is still open.
pitfalls: Thickening the horizontal and vertical strokes by the same amount.
Adding weight without touching the terminals, which then look too small for the new weight.
Keeping the same spacing in the bold because it is easier.

lessons.title: Width, slant and the axes you will not ship
lessons.objective: Extend the design along the axes you have committed to, and understand what each one costs.

principles.title: Width changes the colour, not just the shape
principles.body: Stretching a typeface does not only make it wider: it makes the white inside the letters relatively larger, so the same drawing reads as a lighter weight. That is why a stretched font always looks thin, and why a real condensed has to be redrawn with more weight and a lower x-height.

principles.title: A digital slant is not an italic
principles.body: Slanting a roman produces something that is nearly right and clearly wrong, especially in round and diagonal strokes: the joins break, the strokes thin out unevenly and the shapes lose their construction. A true italic is drawn with a continuous stroke, which changes the letters themselves. Draw it.

principles.title: Optical size is a real design decision
principles.body: As type gets smaller, contrast drops, the x-height rises, spacing opens, apertures close and the fine detail disappears. As type gets bigger the reverse happens, and the weight of the joints can be thinned while the shape stays. A family designed for one size and used at another always looks slightly wrong.

principles.title: Joints are not the same as thins
principles.body: The stroke that joins two curves is a different element from the thin of a high-contrast face, and it can be treated separately. A typeface with low contrast and very thin joints has a texture that shimmers, and it is a legitimate and increasingly common direction.

principles.title: The axes have names, and the names are standard
principles.body: Weight is wght, width is wdth, slant is slnt, optical size is opsz, and roman against italic is ital. Using the registered names means your typeface behaves the way the reader's software expects: a reader can ask for a heavier weight and get one, instead of guessing from the family name.

principles.title: Each axis doubles the number of sources
principles.body: One axis needs two sources: the default and the extreme. Two axes need four, at the corners of the space. Three need eight, and you will spend the rest of your life checking that they agree. The arithmetic is unforgiving, which is why the number of sources is really a decision about how much of your life the family gets.

principles.title: Weight, width and slant are not the same kind of work
principles.body: Weight is the cheapest: a shape can be thickened without being redesigned. Width changes the ratio of white to black, so a condensed has to be redrawn with more weight and a lower x-height. Slant is the most expensive, because a true italic is a different construction rather than a different angle.

practice: Condense your typeface by hand, one letter, and see how much extra weight it needs.
Compare a slanted version of your roman with the way a true italic would be built.
Set your typeface at 8 and at 72 points and mark every place the texture breaks.
Write your axes down with their registered names, and count the sources each one implies.
Draw the four corner sources of a two-axis family and check that the corners look like the same family.
checklist: My condensed is redrawn, not scaled, and carries the right weight.
My italic is drawn as a continuous construction.
I know what my typeface looks like at the smallest and the largest size it will be used.
I use the registered axis names.
I know how many sources each axis I ship costs.
pitfalls: Scaling horizontally and calling it a condensed.
Digitally slanting and calling it an italic.
Designing the text size first and using the same outlines at display size.
Choosing the number of sources by how good the demo looks rather than by how many drawings you can keep in agreement.

lessons.title: Optical sizes
lessons.objective: Understand what changes when a typeface is designed for a different size, and how the optical size axis expresses it.

principles.title: Small sizes want sturdier, larger sizes want finer
principles.body: Going down in size: the weight increases so the tone stays the same, the stroke contrast drops, the letters get slightly wider, the x-height rises, the ascenders and descenders shorten, the apertures open up, the shapes simplify and the serifs get heavier, and the spacing loosens. Going up in size, all of that reverses. The single most important change is the reduction of contrast in the small sizes, and it is sometimes the only one.

principles.title: The axis is measured in points, and the browsers measure in pixels
principles.body: The optical size axis takes the text size in points, and a value between ten and sixteen is recommended as the default for ordinary text. The physical reasoning is a reading distance: a design made for twelve point text at fifteen inches should also work for twenty-four point text at thirty inches. The awkward part is that browsers have no idea how large the screen is, so they match the axis to the size in pixels. The specification says points; the browser says pixels. This is a real, and still unresolved, mismatch — and a good reason to check your typeface on the web rather than to trust the axis.

principles.title: The sizes people actually ask for
principles.body: A useful set of buckets, from the largest to the smallest: display, from forty-eight points up; subhead, fourteen to twenty-four; text, nine to fourteen; and caption, five to nine. Real families put their axis range wherever their designs demand, and the default tends to sit in the text range.

principles.title: What the axis actually changes, measured
principles.body: A survey of the variable fonts that ship an optical size axis found that the stem weight, the contrast, the width and the x-height all move together and in a consistent direction across almost every family: as the size grows, the stems get lighter, the contrast widens, the letters get wider and the x-height shrinks. The cap height barely moves. If your axis does not do that, you have probably drawn a weight axis and named it an optical one.

principles.title: What x-height should be
principles.body: Measured across a wide range of real text families, the x-height sits between a third and a little over half of the em, with a median just above one half. Measured against the cap height instead, it runs from about sixty-two per cent in an old-style serif to about seventy-five per cent in the geometric sans serifs. Two thirds of the cap height is a good place to start, and then you check it on the page.

practice: Set your typeface at eight points and at forty-eight points and mark every place the texture breaks.
Make a small version of your typeface: heavier, lower contrast, bigger x-height, looser. Compare the two as paragraphs.
Compare the x-height of three text fonts you own, as a fraction of the cap height, and decide what you want yours to be.
checklist: I know what my typeface looks like at the smallest and the largest size it will be used.
I can say what changes between a text size and a display size in your own design.
I have checked the x-height of my typeface against a real number.
pitfalls: Drawing one set of outlines and using them at every size, and calling the result a family.
Adding an optical size axis that is really a weight axis, and paying twice the file size for it.

lessons.title: Designing for interpolation
lessons.objective: Make the shapes in your family able to blend, and know what will not blend.

principles.title: The rules for compatible shapes
principles.body: Two shapes can only be interpolated if they have the same number of points, the points are in the same order, the contours start in the same place and run in the same direction, and the handles are compatible. A shape that is not compatible does not break loudly: it breaks quietly, and you find out in the middle of the weight range.

principles.title: Compatible does not mean identical
principles.body: The same number of points is not enough: they have to correspond. If you add a point to one master you must add a point to all of them, in the same place, even if that point does nothing in some of them. This is why the number of points in a source is a design decision and not a by-product.

principles.title: Check the middle, not the ends
principles.body: The extremes of a family are usually drawn and reviewed. The instances in between are generated, and they are where the failure shows: a counter that closes, a stem that thins unevenly, a terminal that changes shape halfway. Proof the middle weights.

principles.title: The number of sources is the real budget
principles.body: Every source is a set of drawings you have to make and keep consistent. Nine sources means nine drawings of every character, and the consistency checking grows faster than the drawing does. Choose the number of sources for the family you will actually finish.

principles.title: Equal counts are not enough
principles.body: Two shapes can have the same number of points and still be unable to blend, because the points do not correspond: the machine can connect the outside of one outline to the counter of the other. The property you need is called topological stability, and equal counts do not establish it. The symptoms are crossed relation lines, a counter that collapses in the middle of the range, and a corner appearing where a smooth join used to be.

principles.title: Do not let the tool fix compatibility for you
principles.body: Automatic reconciliation guesses which point matches which. On a glyph whose masters genuinely differ by design, a guess can pair the wrong contours and produce an ugly blend that still passes the compatibility check. Use the tool to report the mismatch; decide the correspondence yourself.

principles.title: Overlaps must survive the trip into a variable font
principles.body: Desktop production removes overlapping contours, because overlapping shapes can render badly at small sizes and confuse the rasteriser. In a variable font the opposite is true: removing an overlap in one master and not in another changes the point counts and breaks the interpolation. Overlapping contours are explicitly allowed in variable fonts, and if you do remove them, remove them identically everywhere.

principles.title: The anchors have to correspond too
principles.body: A top anchor in one master must be the top anchor in the next, or the accents move as the weight changes. The vertical metrics of the family are a different matter entirely: they are held constant across the masters and are not interpolated at all.

principles.title: Some changes cannot be interpolated
principles.body: A serifed I that has to become a plain I somewhere along the weight range is a discontinuity, and a continuous axis cannot express it. It is expressed as a substitution rule instead: a pair of glyphs and the conditions under which one replaces the other. The rule is applied at run time, which means the swapped glyph has to be referenced correctly by every component and every kerning pair.

principles.title: Design the extremes first
principles.body: Draw the most extreme masters first and establish their point structure as you go, then keep every other master synchronised to it. A family whose extremes were designed together blends; a family whose extremes were designed years apart does not.

practice: Compare the point counts of two letters of your typeface. If they differ, decide which is right before you build a family.
Interpolate between your regular and your bold and look at the middle. Is the counter still open?
Draw one character at every extreme of your design space and check the points line up.
Blend between your two extremes and look at the middle of the range: is any counter closing, is any corner appearing?
Compare the point counts of two glyphs across all your masters. Any difference has to be fixed before the family is worth building.
Draw one character at every corner of your design space and check that the points line up.
checklist: Every character has the same point count in every source of my family.
My contours are in the same order and direction in every source.
I have proofed the interpolated middle weights, not just the extremes.
I know how many sources I have committed to.
Every character has the same point count in every source.
The contours are in the same order and direction in every source.
My anchors correspond by name across the masters.
I have proofed the interpolated middle weights, not just the extremes.
I have not removed an overlap in one master and not in another.
pitfalls: Adding a point to one source and not the others.
Reviewing only the masters.
Committing to a large family because the axes look good on paper.
Trusting a compatibility report that says the counts match. It does not check that the points correspond.
Removing overlaps in the desktop build and keeping them in the variable build, or the other way round.
fontra: The font overview shows your masters side by side: use it to check that the extremes agree.

phases.title: Shipping
phases.goal: Turn a finished design into a released typeface that works for the people who will use it.
phases.why: The design is the easy, enjoyable part. Everything after it is production, and it is where most projects actually die.
phases.milestone: The typeface is released, and you know what it will be used for and what it will not.

lessons.title: What production actually means
lessons.objective: Know what has to happen between a finished drawing and a font somebody can install.

principles.title: Production is a checklist, not a creative phase
principles.body: Interlocking the components, applying the vertical metrics, building the OpenType features, setting the name records, exporting in every format you intend to ship, and testing the result on the platforms you care about. None of it is design work, and all of it has to be done.

principles.title: Components are a promise
principles.body: A component is a piece of a glyph stored separately so that it can be shared and moved together. If you ship components, you are promising that when the designer moves the top of an accented capital, the accent moves with it. Components that do not behave that way are worse than no components.

principles.title: OpenType features are a design decision
principles.body: Ligatures, alternates, fractions, small capitals and stylistic sets are not extras to be sprinkled on at the end. Each one is a claim about what the typeface can do, and each one adds to the kerning, the testing and the support you have to provide afterwards.

principles.title: Test on the platforms you will be used on
principles.body: A font that works in your editor may fall apart in a browser, on a phone, or in a word processor. Test the real file, on the real platforms, at the real sizes, before you announce anything.

principles.title: The project starts as sources, not as a binary
principles.body: The first thing to set up is the family itself: every master and every instance you intend to ship, the naming scheme, and the build that produces the file. Setting the build up early, including the hinting stage, means the typeface is testable from the first day instead of at the end, when a problem is expensive.

principles.title: The quality gate is different for a new family and for an update
principles.body: A new family is checked for consistency between the styles, the quality of the outlines, the basic spacing and kerning, and for nothing strange happening. An update is checked for regressions instead: no text reflowing, no shaping bug introduced, no big changes in the font tables, no change to the vertical metrics, and nothing changed that cannot be explained. The second list is much stricter, and it is the one that amateur releases fail.

principles.title: Rebuild, do not ship the export
principles.body: The binaries that come out of a font editor are a starting point, not the artefact. The accepted practice at the largest open font libraries is to rebuild every release from the sources with a single toolchain, so that every family in the collection is produced the same way and a mistake can be fixed once.

principles.title: A release is a bundle, not a file
principles.body: A release carries the font files in the formats you promised, the licence text, a changelog, a readme, and a version number that matches the tag. The packaging is part of the work, and it is the part most often skipped.

practice: Write the production checklist for your own project before you start drawing, and tick it as you go.
Export your typeface and install it on a second machine. If it only works in your working copy, it does not work.
Set a paragraph in the exported font in a browser and in a word processor and compare them with your proof.
Write the release checklist for your own project: what files, what formats, what licence, what changelog, what version.
Test the exported font on a machine that is not the one you drew it on.
Diff your typeface against the previous release and write down every difference you can find. Anything you cannot explain is a bug.
checklist: I have a production checklist for my project and it is finished.
The exported file is tested outside my editor.
Every feature I ship works as advertised.
I know which platforms and applications the typeface is for.
I have a release checklist and it is finished.
The exported file is tested outside my editor.
I have diffed this release against the last one and explained every difference.
The version number in the file matches the release.
pitfalls: Building features nobody asked for and nobody will use.
Shipping components that do not move together.
Testing only the working copy inside the editor you drew in.
Shipping the file straight out of the editor.
Releasing without checking that the change you made did not change anything else.

lessons.title: Releasing, and knowing when to stop
lessons.objective: Get the typeface out, and recognise the moment when it is finished.

principles.title: Release early, release often
principles.body: Putting a partial family out while it is still growing gets you feedback, gets you income, and keeps the project alive. It also means that everything you learn goes into the next version rather than into a private file nobody sees.

principles.title: Everything is done, at a different version
principles.body: A typeface never really finishes. Styles are added, languages are supported, mistakes are fixed. The useful question is not whether it is perfect but whether it is good enough to be used, and that question gets easier to answer the longer you look at it.

principles.title: Enthusiasm is the signal
principles.body: When you can no longer justify more work on a project, that is how you know it is done. And when you are stuck, Save As: a clean version on disk, with the critic temporarily silenced, often frees you to move again.

principles.title: Nothing is destructive
principles.body: Editing outlines is not like erasing a drawing. A repositioned point and a saved version can go a very long way towards reviving a project you thought was finished.

practice: Put your current state out somewhere, even if it is only four styles and a few characters.
Make a list of the things you are still unhappy with, and decide which of them would actually stop somebody from using it.
Save a version of the project before you start a change you are not sure about.
checklist: There is a version of this typeface that other people can use.
I have a list of what is still open, and I know which of those matter.
I have not abandoned a project that could still be good.
pitfalls: Waiting for perfection that never arrives.
Polishing instead of shipping when the typeface is already good enough.
Abandoning a project in a low week instead of saving a version and coming back to it.
fontra: Export the font from the font info panel when you are ready to share it.

lessons.title: Type design as a profession
lessons.objective: Understand how the work is paid for, scoped and valued, so that you can make realistic plans.

principles.title: There are two kinds of work
principles.body: A foundry typeface is a contribution to a catalogue and it earns over years, through licences. A commissioned typeface is a project with a client, a deadline, a scope and a fee. The skills overlap; the working methods do not, and confusing the two is how young designers end up working for years without being paid.

principles.title: Scope is the deliverable
principles.body: Before anything is drawn, agree: how many characters, how many styles, which languages, which OpenType features, which formats, who owns the artwork, what the licence covers, when it is due and what it costs. Most professional disputes are scope disputes that were never spoken aloud.

principles.title: Price the whole family, not the drawing
principles.body: The drawing is a fraction of the cost. The multiplication by styles and by languages, the kerning, the production, the testing and the support afterwards are the rest. Quote the family, not the first style.

principles.title: Proofs are how you get paid for the thinking
principles.body: A client cannot judge a typeface by looking at outlines. They judge it by reading it, in their own words, at their own size. A good proof is the document that makes the value of the work legible, and it is worth as much as the drawing.

principles.title: A practice, not a sprint
principles.body: Type design is roughly five per cent creativity and ninety-five per cent production. The people who get good at it are the ones who can stay with the production part, and they are the ones who ship.

principles.title: The two markets price the same work in completely different ways
principles.body: Retail is priced per style or per seat, and it earns slowly over years: a single style from a retail foundry commonly runs somewhere between thirty and eighty dollars, and the money arrives as a trickle rather than a payment. Commission work is priced as a project: hourly rates around eighty dollars, or a fixed fee that starts around ten thousand for a focused single-master design and rises steeply with every extra master and every extra language.

principles.title: The master is the unit of price
principles.body: A custom family quoted by master puts a family with three masters at roughly three times the price of one, and the figure quoted by one foundry was fifteen thousand per master. This is why the scope conversation, and not the drawing, decides what a commission costs.

principles.title: Time is priced too
principles.body: A single weight takes three to five months. A full multi-weight family with scripts takes nine to eighteen. A typical family is three to nine months depending on scope. These are not the designer being slow; they are what the multiplication of styles, languages, kerning and testing actually adds up to.

principles.title: Value-based licensing has overtaken seats and views
principles.body: More and more independent foundries price by the size of the licensing company rather than by the number of people using the font, charging once and for all. The argument is that a company with five thousand staff gets more value from the typeface than a company with five, and that per-seat pricing punishes exactly the organisations that can afford to commission work.

principles.title: Selling unfinished work is a model, not a compromise
principles.body: The platform that sells fonts in progress lets the designer set the price, keeps a share, and raises the price as the work completes; the early buyers get every update for free, and every release carries notes on how far along it is. It also keeps the catalogue alive with something new, and it pays the designer before the family is finished, which is when the money is most needed.

principles.title: What the client owns is worth writing down
principles.body: The usual arrangement is that the foundry keeps the copyright and the client gets exclusive use for a period or for a market. Some foundries will license exclusively and not sell the family at all during the licence. This is the part of the contract that decides what the work is worth later, and it is the part that is easiest to leave vague.

practice: Write a scope document for a typeface you would like to be commissioned, with a number of styles, a character count and a price.
Count the hours you actually spent on the last project and compare them with the hours you drew. Write the ratio down.
Look at the licences of five fonts you own and see how many different models are in use.
Price a two-master family for a client by the hour, and then by the master, and see how far apart the two answers are.
Write a scope document for a family you would like to be commissioned: the styles, the character count, the languages, the features, the formats, the licence, the deadline and the fee.
Look at the licences of five fonts you own and see how many different pricing models are in use.

I can write a scope for a family, with a price.
I know what my licence grants and what it does not.
I can make a proof that shows a client what they are buying.

Starting a family before the client has agreed what the family is.

glossary.definition: The opening left by a curve: the gap of a c, the mouth of an e, the opening of an a. Small apertures look tidy at text size and turn into dark holes at display size.
The part of a letter that rises above the x-height: b, d, f, h, k, l. It separates those letters from the capitals and from the figures.
The diagonal through the thickest points of a round letter, which shows where the stress of the curve falls.
The line on which the letters sit. Everything in a typeface is measured from it and against it.
A heavier style of a family. It is also the best test of a design: drawing it shows you which decisions were accidental.
A curved stroke that closes back on itself. The b, d, p and q share one bowl; the a and the g each have their own.
The line the capitals reach. Ascenders usually rise slightly above it.
A shared piece of a glyph stored separately so that it can be moved together with the letters that use it. A promise that has to be kept.
The difference in thickness between the thick and thin parts of a stroke. The eye reads horizontals as heavier than verticals, so a true contrast is never as extreme as it looks on the drawing.
Whether the thick and thin come from the movement of the tool or from pressure on it: translation (broad nib) or expansion (pointed pen). Most typefaces are one, or a hybrid.
The enclosed white space inside a letter. It is the first thing to close up when the weight goes up, and the first thing to rescue a small size.
The interior angle where two strokes meet: the point of the V, the upper joints of the W, the meeting of the diagonals in the Y.
The horizontal stroke that crosses a letter. It sits above centre in the H and below centre in the A, and both positions are deliberate.
The part of a letter that falls below the baseline: g, j, p, q, y. It separates those letters from the baseline itself.
The region of the possible that a typeface occupies: its weights, widths, slants and sizes. Also the region a designer explores while sketching.
The roman form of the lowercase a, with a bowl and a shoulder. The single-storey form is the italic and the sans alternative.
The small stroke that turns the top of a g into a spur or a loop. It is a small feature with a large effect on the letter's personality.
An ascender or a descender. The two do different jobs and do not have to be the same length.
A contrast model in which the thick and thin come from pressure on a pointed pen. Bodoni and Didot are expansion designs.
The highest, lowest, leftmost and rightmost points of a curve. Putting a point there makes the handles leave horizontally or vertically, which makes the curve easy to edit.
A numeral. Lining figures sit on the baseline and the cap height; old-style figures have ascenders and descenders.
One drawn character, as stored in the font. The character you type is not always the glyph you get.
The point on a curve where it changes from bending one way to bending the other, as in the middle of an S. A point there lets you shape both halves independently.
The machine blending between two drawn shapes to make the styles in between. It only works if the shapes are compatible: same point count, same order, same direction.
The adjustment of the space between a particular pair of letters, applied after the sidebearings. It is a patch, not a design.
The bowl of a capital P, when it is distinguished from the bowl of a B.
The size a typeface is meant to be read at. It changes contrast, x-height, spacing, apertures and the size of the fine detail.
The small amount by which a round or pointed letter passes above or below a metric line, so that it looks the same size as its flat neighbours.
The effect by which a vertical stroke next to a diagonal appears to lean. The X is where it is strongest, and the correction is to make the true verticals slightly unequal.

The relationship between the parts of a letter. Classical proportions make the round capitals circles and the flat capitals about twice as tall as wide; modern proportions make the capitals more nearly equal in width.
A document that tests a typeface and shows its problems. A proof answers what the design is trying to solve, what is wrong with it and what could be done about it.
The curve that joins two stems in an n, m or h, and the equivalent join on the letters with a bowl.
The space to the left and right of a letter, outside its outline. It is what determines how the letter sits next to its neighbours.
A shape that is drawn by hand. The styles in between are generated from the sources, so every source is a set of drawings you have to keep in agreement.
The main curved stroke of an s. Where the s is thickest is a decision, not an accident.
The main vertical stroke of a letter. Its thickness defines the weight of the whole typeface.
Where a curved stroke is thickest. It comes from the tool, and it is what makes a c look different from a mirror of it.
Where a stroke ends. A terminal can be flat, angled, round, flared or carry a serif, and the choice changes the voice of the whole family.
The dot of an i and a j. Where the capital I is dotted, the tittle is wider than the stem.
A contrast model in which the thick and thin come from the constant angle of a broad nib, so only the direction of travel changes the weight. Jenson and blackletter are translation designs.
The bottom point of a V. A sharp vertex must dip below the baseline or it reads as blunt.
How heavy the strokes are. It is the cheapest parameter to change and the one that most changes how a typeface reads.
How wide the letters are. Changing it also changes the ratio of white to black, so a condensed has to be redrawn rather than squeezed.
The height of the lowercase, named after the x, which is usually the only lowercase letter with neither ascender nor descender. It is usually around two thirds of the cap height.
